title: Concurrent Flame Spread Modeling using Flamelet Generated Manifolds in Microgravity with Comparison to BASS Experiments using Two-Color Tomography

summary.text: A modeling investigation that aims to develop and validate flamelet generated manifold techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity, using BASS and BASS-II experiments as benchmarks.

fuels.text: Polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) rod samples and wax cylinders, among BASS geometries.

geometry.text: BASS geometries including flat sheets, spheres, rod-shaped PMMA samples and wax cylinders.

measurements.text: Flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction and flame spread rate, with soot and temperature fields reconstructed by two-color tomography from DSLR imagery.

hardware.text: DSLR cameras used for two-color tomography of existing BASS and BASS-II imagery.

claims.text: The research aims to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity.
The research aims to use the BASS and BASS-II experiments as benchmarks.
The investigation hypothesizes that the unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach can accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity.
The stated long-term goal is to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials.

limitations.text: The investigation is computational and uses existing BASS and BASS-II imagery; the metadata states no validation result.
This draft cites PSI metadata; no PDF text or experimental-table passages were processed for this investigation.

evidence.excerpt: The objective of this research was to develop and validate new flamelet generated manifold (FGM) modeling techniques for concurrent flame spread in microgravity.
using the NASA Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) experiments as benchmarks
the long-term goal was to enable accurate prediction of flammability limits for spacecraft materials
The unsteady flamelet generated manifold (UFGM) approach was believed to be able to accurately reproduce concurrent flame spread in microgravity
the unsteady FGM method was implemented and tested on various BASS geometries, including flat sheets, spheres, and rod-shaped polymethyl methacrylate (PMMA) samples, as well as wax cylinders.

Experimental imagery found in PSI from the BASS and BASS-II investigations was post-processed using newly developed two-color tomography methods with DSLR cameras, enabling 3D reconstructions of soot and temperature fields for direct comparison to model predictions.
The evaluation metrics included flame geometry, temperature distribution, soot volume fraction, and flame spread rate
The computational methods being refined have the potential to enable more effective fire prevention and mitigation strategies
